s1.syndrome_frame: Progressive respiratory distress with pleural effusion and mediastino-pulmonary mass
salient_findings: Mediastino-pulmonary mass in the left upper lobe
Endobronchial lesion in the left upper-lobe bronchus
key_facts: 40-year-old woman
One month postpartum
No significant past medical history
Three weeks of symptoms
General health deterioration
Signs of left pleural effusion on examination
Homogeneous opacity occupying the entire left hemithorax with mediastinal shift on chest radiograph
Serial thoracenteses produced approximately 2 L of serous fluid every three days
Thoracic ultrasonography confirmed large pleural effusion
Ultrasound-guided pleural biopsy was non-diagnostic
Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 104 × 102 × 141 mm mediastino-pulmonary mass
Mass contacts the subclavian artery and lateral border of the aorta and encases a branch of the left pulmonary artery
Bronchoscopic examination showed an endobronchial lesion
Endobronchial biopsies were non-contributory on two occasions

shortlist.label: Non-small cell lung cancer
shortlist.why_kept: Presence of a large mediastino-pulmonary mass and pleural effusion

shortlist.label: Small cell lung cancer
shortlist.why_kept: Rapid progression of symptoms and presence of a large mediastino-pulmonary mass

shortlist.label: Lymphoma
shortlist.why_kept: Presence of a large mediastino-pulmonary mass and pleural effusion, with potential for rapid progression

shortlist.label: Pancoast tumor
shortlist.why_kept: Location of the mass in the left upper lobe and presence of an endobronchial lesion

shortlist.label: Mesothelioma
shortlist.why_kept: Presence of a large pleural effusion and a mediastino-pulmonary mass, with potential for malignancy

raw.rationale: The presence of a large mediastino-pulmonary mass with an endobronchial lesion and significant pleural effusion, as seen on imaging and bronchoscopic examination, is most consistent with a diagnosis of non-small cell lung cancer, which is a common cause of these findings.

rejected.label: Small cell lung cancer
rejected.why: While possible, small cell lung cancer tends to be more aggressive and centrally located, often with more pronounced systemic symptoms and paraneoplastic syndromes, which are not highlighted in the vignette.

rejected.label: Lymphoma
rejected.why: Lymphoma can cause mediastinal masses and pleural effusions, but the presence of an endobronchial lesion and the specific characteristics of the mass are less typical for lymphoma.

rejected.label: Pancoast tumor
rejected.why: Pancoast tumors are located at the lung apex and typically cause shoulder and arm pain due to invasion of the brachial plexus, which is not mentioned in the case.

rejected.label: Mesothelioma
rejected.why: Mesothelioma usually presents with diffuse pleural thickening and effusion, and while it can cause a mass, the presence of an endobronchial lesion and the specific mass characteristics are not typical for mesothelioma.
